subject: Advanced Electronics

questions.text: Define slew rate of an operational amplifier. An op-amp has a slew rate of $0.5\text{ V}/\mu\text{s}$ and closed-loop gain of $33$. The input signal is given by $v_{in} = 0.01\sin(10^6 t) + 0.05\sin(350 \times 10^3 t)$ (or $0.1\sin(200000 t)$). Determine whether the output is distorted due to slew rate limitation. If so, suggest a remedy.

Why is the output current of a simple current mirror circuit not exactly equal to reference current? Derive an expression for the current gain and output resistance of a Widlar current source with necessary circuit diagrams.

What are the advantages of an R-2R ladder DAC over a binary-weighted resistor DAC? Derive the expression for the output voltage of an inverted R-2R ladder DAC and show that the output voltage ranges from $0$ to $-V_{\text{ref}}$.
Explain the working of a Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC in brief with a suitable example for a 6-bit ADC with $V_{\text{ref}} = 16\text{ V}$ and $V_{in} = 10.25\text{ V}$.

Explain the operation of a Dual-Slope Integrating ADC with circuit diagram, timing waveforms, and mathematical derivation. An 8-bit dual slope ADC has $R = 20\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C = 0.001\ \mu\text{F}$. An analog input of $-0.25\text{ V}$ is integrated for $T_1 = 150\ \mu\text{s}$. (a) What is the maximum integrator voltage reached? (b) If switched to $+5\text{ V}$ reference, how long does it take to reach $0\text{ V}$? (c) If clock is $3.125\text{ MHz}$, what is the digital output?
List out characteristics and application areas of an Instrumentation Amplifier. Derive the expression for the differential voltage gain of a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier.
Define input bias current and input offset current of an op-amp. What is their effect on the output voltage? How can the effect of input bias current be reduced or compensated in an op-amp circuit?
What are the advantages of a transistor logarithmic amplifier over a diode logarithmic amplifier? Derive the output voltage expression of a logarithmic amplifier using a matched transistor pair.
Implement the mathematical expression $V_o = V_1^2 + V_2^2 - V_1 \sqrt{V_2}$ (or $V_o = V_1^2 - V_2^2 + V_1 V_2$) using log, antilog, summer, and subtractor op-amp circuits.
Draw the detailed circuit diagram of a four-quadrant analog multiplier and derive its input-output relationship using log and antilog circuits.
Explain the working principle and two-transistor analogy (model) of a Silicon Controlled Rectifier (SCR). Sketch its V-I characteristics curve and discuss its turn-on and turn-off mechanisms.
Explain the operation of a step-down (Buck) chopper for RLE load with the help of mathematical equations and waveforms. Show that maximum ripple current is present when duty cycle $k = 0.5$.

questions.chapter: Switched Mode Power Supplies and Drives
questions.text: A Buck-Boost regulator has an input voltage $V_s = 12\text{ V}$, duty cycle $k = 0.25$, and switching frequency $f = 25\text{ kHz}$. Inductance $L = 150\ \mu\text{H}$ and filter capacitance $C = 220\ \mu\text{F}$. Determine: (a) The average output voltage $V_a$, (b) The peak-to-peak output ripple voltage $\Delta V_c$, (c) The peak-to-peak ripple current of inductor $\Delta I$, and (d) The critical values of $L$ and $C$.
Define chopper and inverter. Explain the working of a single-phase full-bridge inverter with necessary circuit diagrams and waveforms.
Show that the voltage gain of a differential amplifier with active load is twice that of a differential amplifier with passive load.
List out applications of isolation amplifiers. Explain the operation of an optically coupled isolation amplifier and a transformer-coupled isolation amplifier.

Derive the voltage gain $A_v = \left(1 + \frac{2 R_1}{R_g}\right)\left(\frac{R_3}{R_2}\right)$ and Common-Mode Rejection Ratio (CMRR) of a three-op-amp Instrumentation Amplifier. Why does it provide exceptionally high input impedance and high CMRR without matched source impedances?
questions.solutionOutline: First stage consists of two non-inverting buffers cross-coupled via gain-setting resistor R_g. Input impedance is op-amp non-inverting terminal impedance (gigohms). Differential gain of stage 1 is A_d1 = 1 + 2 R1 / R_g; common-mode gain is A_cm1 = 1 (amplifies difference while passing common-mode unity). Second stage is difference amplifier with gain R3 / R2, rejecting common-mode voltage. CMRR is multiplied by stage-1 differential gain.

questions.text: Explain Isolation Amplifiers. Compare Transformer-Coupled, Optically-Coupled, and Capacitively-Coupled isolation amplifiers with respect to barrier breakdown voltage, common-mode rejection, and medical bio-potential isolation applications.
questions.solutionOutline: Provides complete galvanic isolation (thousands of volts) between input and output grounds, breaking ground loops and protecting patients/sensitive instrumentation. Transformer coupling uses modulator/demodulator with high-frequency carrier (20-100 kHz) across toroidal transformer barrier. Optical coupling uses matched linear optocoupler LEDs and photodiodes. Capacitive coupling uses differential digital modulator across low-capacitance ceramic barrier (high CMRR and bandwidth).

questions.text: Derive the output voltage of a Translog (BJT-based) Logarithmic Amplifier: $v_o = -V_T \ln\left(\frac{v_i}{I_s R}\right)$. Explain why uncompensated log amplifiers suffer severe temperature drift due to $V_T$ and $I_s$, and describe the dual-transistor temperature compensation circuit.
questions.solutionOutline: BJT in feedback loop of op-amp with base grounded (v_B = 0). Collector current I_c = I_s [exp(v_BE / V_T) - 1] approx I_s exp(v_BE / V_T). Inverting virtual ground sets I_c = v_i / R. Output v_o = -v_BE = -V_T ln(v_i / (I_s R)). Temperature drift: I_s doubles every 5 deg C; thermal voltage V_T = k T / q is proportional to absolute temperature. Compensated by subtracting reference log output v_o2 = -V_T ln(V_ref / (I_s R_ref)) using matched dual BJT (cancels I_s) and PTAT thermistor (cancels V_T).

questions.text: Design an Analog Multiplier and Divider circuit using Log and Anti-log amplifiers and summing op-amps based on the mathematical identity $\ln(v_1 v_2) = \ln v_1 + \ln v_2$ and $\ln(v_1 / v_2) = \ln v_1 - \ln v_2$.
questions.solutionOutline: Multiplier: Input voltages v1, v2 fed into log amplifiers producing -K ln(v1) and -K ln(v2). Summing amplifier computes -(-K ln v1 - K ln v2) = K ln(v1 * v2). Output fed to anti-log amplifier (BJT in input path, resistor in feedback) which computes exp(ln(v1 * v2)) = v1 * v2. Divider uses differential subtraction: log(v1) - log(v2) = log(v1 / v2) prior to anti-log stage. Requires positive unipolar inputs (single-quadrant operation).

questions.text: Explain the Analog Four-Quadrant Gilbert Multiplier Cell. Derive the differential output current as a function of the hyperbolic tangent of differential input voltages: $I_{out} = I_0 \tanh\left(\frac{v_1}{2V_T}\right)\tanh\left(\frac{v_2}{2V_T}\right)$.
questions.solutionOutline: Cross-coupled differential pairs of BJTs. Lower pair splits tail current I_0 into I_1, I_2 based on differential input v1: I_1 - I_2 = I_0 tanh(v1 / 2V_T). Upper cross-coupled pairs modulate currents based on differential input v2: output current Delta I = (I_1 - I_2) tanh(v2 / 2V_T) = I_0 tanh(v1 / 2V_T) tanh(v2 / 2V_T). For small signals v1, v2 << 2V_T: tanh(x) approx x, giving linear true 4-quadrant multiplication v_out proportional to v1 * v2.

questions.text: Explain R-2R Ladder Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) in voltage and current modes. Derive the output voltage $V_o = -V_{ref} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{b_i}{2^i}$. Why is the R-2R ladder preferred over binary weighted-resistor DACs for high resolution (12-16 bits)?
questions.solutionOutline: Uses only two resistor values (R and 2R). Thevenin equivalent resistance looking into each node is always R. Node voltages divide by factor of 2 at each progressive ladder stage. Binary switches direct currents to virtual ground summing bus of op-amp. Output V_o = -V_ref sum b_i 2^(-i). Preferred because binary weighted DAC requires 2^n resistor spread (e.g. 1k to 64M for 16-bit), which is impossible to track accurately on monolithic ICs over temperature; R-2R needs only 2:1 matching.

questions.text: Explain Dual-Slope Integrating Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). Derive the relation showing conversion result $N = \frac{V_{in}}{V_{ref}} 2^n$ is independent of integrator $R, C$ values and clock frequency drift. Why is it used in digital multimeters?
questions.solutionOutline: Run-up phase: switch connects V_in to integrator for fixed clock counts N1 = 2^n (time T1): V_peak = -V_in T1 / (RC). Run-down phase: switch connects -V_ref; integrator ramps back to 0 in counts N2 (time T2): V_peak = V_ref T2 / (RC). Equating gives V_in T1 = V_ref T2 => N2 = N1 (V_in / V_ref). R, C, and clock frequency f cancel out completely. Integrating over period T1 = 20 ms provides infinite rejection of 50 Hz AC power line hum.

questions.text: Explain Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC. Detail the binary search conversion sequence with D/A converter, sample-and-hold circuit, and comparator. Calculate conversion time for an 8-bit SAR ADC clocked at $2\text{ MHz}$.
questions.solutionOutline: Performs binary search. Sample-and-hold freezes analog input. SAR tests bits from MSB (bit n-1) to LSB (bit 0). Sets trial bit to 1, internal DAC generates trial analog voltage. Comparator tests if V_in >= V_DAC: if yes, trial bit remains 1; if no, trial bit resets to 0. Takes exactly n clock cycles for n bits. For 8 bits at f_clk = 2 MHz: clock period T = 0.5 us; conversion time T_conv = 8 * 0.5 us = 4.0 us (plus 1 sample cycle = 4.5 us).

questions.text: Describe Sigma-Delta ($\Sigma\Delta$) ADC architecture: Over-sampling ($f_s \gg 2 f_B$), 1-bit DAC/ADC, Noise Shaping with loop integrator, and Digital Decimation Filter. Why do Sigma-Delta ADCs achieve ultra-high 24-bit resolution at audio frequencies?
questions.solutionOutline: Over-samples input by large factor OSR = f_s / (2 f_B). Modulator subtracts 1-bit DAC output from input, integrates difference, and quantizes via 1-bit comparator. Integrator acts as high-pass filter for quantization noise (Noise Shaping), pushing quantization noise power out of audio band into high frequencies. Digital decimation lowpass filter filters out high-frequency noise and down-samples to Nyquist rate, yielding 16-24 bit resolution without precision analog resistors.

questions.chapter: Switched Mode Power Supplies and Drives
questions.text: Explain the Buck (Step-Down) DC-DC Converter. Derive the continuous conduction mode (CCM) voltage conversion ratio $V_o / V_s = D$, inductor current ripple $\Delta I_L$, and the minimum critical inductance $L_{min}$ to avoid discontinuous conduction.
questions.solutionOutline: Switch closed for duration D*T: inductor voltage v_L = V_s - V_o; inductor current ramps up by Delta I_L = (V_s - V_o) D T / L. Switch open for (1-D)T: diode conducts, v_L = -V_o; inductor current ramps down by Delta I_L = V_o (1 - D) T / L. Volt-second balance (V_s - V_o) D = V_o (1 - D) => V_o = D * V_s. Continuous conduction requires minimum average current I_L >= Delta I_L / 2 => L_min = (1 - D) R / (2 f).

questions.chapter: Switched Mode Power Supplies and Drives
questions.text: Explain Boost (Step-Up) and Buck-Boost DC-DC Converters. Derive their output voltage conversion ratios $V_o / V_s = \frac{1}{1 - D}$ and $V_o / V_s = -\frac{D}{1 - D}$, sketch inductor current waveforms, and calculate capacitor voltage ripple.
questions.solutionOutline: Boost converter: switch on charges inductor from V_s; switch off delivers stored energy in series with input through diode to load: V_s D T + (V_s - V_o)(1 - D) T = 0 => V_o = V_s / (1 - D) > V_s. Buck-boost converter: switch on stores energy in inductor; switch off inverts polarity across load: V_s D T + (-V_o)(1 - D) T = 0 => V_o = -V_s * [D / (1 - D)]. Output voltage ripple Delta V_o = I_o D / (f C).

questions.chapter: Switched Mode Power Supplies and Drives
questions.text: Explain Isolated SMPS Topologies: Flyback Converter and Forward Converter. Contrast transformer core demagnetization (tertiary reset winding), transformer utilization, and peak transistor stress in offline power supplies.
questions.solutionOutline: Flyback is isolated buck-boost: energy stored in coupled inductor (gapped core) during switch on; delivered to secondary when switch turns off; low cost for <150W supplies. Forward converter is isolated buck: energy transferred directly to secondary when switch is on via un-gapped transformer. Forward converter requires tertiary demagnetizing winding and diode to reset core flux to zero during off-time, preventing core saturation.

questions.text: Explain the Silicon Controlled Rectifier (SCR / Thyristor): Two-transistor analogy (p-n-p and n-p-n regenerative feedback), turn-on mechanisms, latching vs holding currents, and turn-off commutation techniques (Natural vs Forced commutation).
questions.solutionOutline: Four-layer p-n-p-n device modeled as coupled PNP (Q1) and NPN (Q2) transistors. Anode current I_A = (alpha2 I_g + I_co1 + I_co2) / [1 - (alpha1 + alpha2)]. Gate pulse injects I_g, driving loop gain alpha1 + alpha2 -> 1, triggering regenerative latch-up into low-resistance conduction. Latching current is minimum anode current to sustain conduction as gate pulse is removed; Holding current is minimum current below which SCR turns off. Commutation turns SCR off by reversing anode-cathode voltage.

questions.chapter: Switched Mode Power Supplies and Drives
questions.text: Explain H-Bridge DC Motor Drives using power MOSFETs/IGBTs. Describe Bipolar and Unipolar Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) switching schemes, shoot-through prevention using dead-time control, and freewheeling diode protection.
questions.solutionOutline: Four semiconductor switches (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4) in H configuration driving motor bi-directionally. Forward: Q1 and Q4 on. Reverse: Q2 and Q3 on. Shoot-through (fatal short circuit) occurs if both high-side Q1 and low-side Q2 turn on simultaneously; prevented by dead-time delay circuitry in gate driver. Bipolar PWM switches diagonals simultaneously (-Vs to +Vs). Unipolar PWM switches legs independently (0 to +Vs). Antiparallel freewheeling diodes clamp inductive kickback V = -L di/dt.
